name: Vegetarian / pescatarian

lead: Vegetarian diets exclude meat and pescatarian diets add fish and seafood; both may include eggs and dairy. They are a moderate middle ground between omnivore and vegan eating, used for leanness, skin and general health.

The chain is a shift toward plants and, for pescatarians, fish-derived omega-3, which improves overall diet quality and can help body composition. Research is observational: a UK Biobank cohort and meta-analysis looked at cancer risk, a Swiss population study at cardiovascular risk factors, and studies of young people compared micronutrient status. None test appearance.

paras: People drop meat, keep eggs, dairy and fish to taste, and build meals around legumes, vegetables, grains and seafood. Many see it as an easier, flexible step than going fully vegan.
Nutrient studies compare B12, iron and others across diets, and vegetarians are advised to watch B12 and iron. Some fish carry mercury and PCBs.

chain: Less meat, more plants and fish
angle.text: Vegetarian and pescatarian diets reduce meat and raise plant and fish intake, which people use to get leaner and support healthier skin. Population data cover health outcomes; looks are not directly studied.

lead: Vegetarian diets exclude meat, and pescatarian diets exclude meat but include fish and seafood; both may include eggs and dairy. The term pescetarian was coined in the UK in the late 1980s and about 3 percent of adults worldwide were estimated to follow this diet in 2017-2018.[1] They are discussed in looksmaxxing contexts as reduced-meat options for skin, leanness and general health.

Research is mostly observational. A UK Biobank cohort and meta-analysis examined meat, vegetarian, pescatarian and fish-poultry diets and cancer risk, a Swiss population study linked these diets to cardiovascular risk factors, and studies of young people compared micronutrient status.[2][3][4][5]
infobox: Fish and seafood, sometimes eggs and dairy

paras: Lacto-ovo vegetarians eat dairy and eggs; lacto vegetarians eat dairy only; ovo vegetarians eat eggs only; vegans eat no animal products; flexitarians eat mostly plants with occasional meat or fish.[1] Pescatarian diets are close to Mediterranean-style eating, which features fish and plants.[1]

In the UK Biobank analysis of 409,110 participants, researchers compared diet types with all-cancer and site-specific cancer incidence, and combined the results with a meta-analysis of prospective cohorts.[2] The Swiss study examined prevalence, sociodemographic features and cardiovascular risk factors among vegetarian, pescatarian and flexitarian dieters.[3]

Studies of Norwegian and Swedish 16-24-year-olds compared micronutrient intake and status, and food groups and biomarkers, across vegan, lacto-ovo-vegetarian, pescatarian and omnivorous diets.[4][6][5] A study of Americans found popular diets differ in carbon footprint and diet quality.[7] Other studies cover nutritional status and habits, thrombotic risk factors and erectile function with organic and fasting regimens.[8][9][10] Modelling research examined diets with reduced animal protein.[11]
Wikipedia notes that some fish contain mercury and PCBs, and that choosing low-mercury fish reduces exposure.[1]

The studies identified are observational or cross-sectional, covering cancer, cardiovascular risk factors, micronutrient status and diet quality.[2][3][4][8][6][5] No clinical trials were found testing vegetarian or pescatarian diets for skin or facial appearance.
No substantial forum discussion specific to these diets was identified; they appear as moderate options between omnivorous and vegan eating.
